newsitem.title: USA: Juror asks to be spared Oklahoma bombing case.
newsitem.headline: Juror asks to be spared Oklahoma bombing case.

text.p: A woman who served on a jury that sentenced a murderer to die asked Thursday to be spared from the Oklahoma City bombing trial, saying she did not want to face the possibility of having to vote for execution again.
"I'm of the opinion that once in a lifetime is enough to have to do that," the woman said, referring to the jury she sat on 15 years ago in Oklahoma City where a man was convicted of rape and murder.
"I feel like I've done my civic duty over my life time," she said on the ninth day of jury deliberation in the bombing case.
She said she worked hard to erase the memory of her jury experience. "I could not even tell you the man's name today," she said, adding she did not even know if he had been executed.
The woman who lived in Oklahoma for many years said she still has ties with her former home and has many friends and relatives who live there, including her son and his family.
She said she has discussed the April 19, 1995 bombing of the Alfred P. Murrah federal building many times with her son.

As has been customary Federal Judge Richard Matsch did not announce if she would be excused from serving. The identity of the jurors has been kept secret and they sit behind a wooden screen out of the sight of spectators in the courtroom.
Jury selection is expected to take another two weeks. The government will then present its case, calling about 320 witnesses, a source close to the trial said.
Another potential juror surprised the courtroom when she described herself as a witch who believes in paganism.

The young mother, whose husband committed suicide in 1993, said she could set aside reservations about the death penalty and would consider it as a possible punishment for Timothy McVeigh who is charged in the bombing that killed 168 people. He has pleaded innocent and faces the death penalty, if convicted.
The woman, who has studied graphic art, said she attended "circles" where people burned incense, danced and sang.
The soft-spoken woman, who paused several times before answering questions, said she first learned about being a witch when she was 12 years old.
"I began to get interested in ghosts and spirits and started reading about paganism," she said, adding that she decided to become a witch after graduating from high school.

The woman said she was raised a Christian and described the Wicca "religion" as a peaceful one whose adherents worshipped gods and goddesses. A Wiccan is a member of a group that practices witchcraft.
Initially, she said the death penalty was never justified but when pressed by prosecutor Larry Mackey the woman said she could set aside her views and vote for the death penalty.
The judge, prosecutors and defence attorneys have questioned 56 people so far as they try to select a jury of 12 plus six alternates.
